sentences: Bare to the waist, wearing an amber necklace and a white cloth at her hips, a woman stands before us.
The German painter Paula Modersohn-Becker painted this self-portrait in Paris on 25 May 1906.
That February she had left her husband, the painter Otto Modersohn, and the artists' colony of Worpswede to devote herself entirely to painting in Paris.
She was thirty when she made this picture.
The 'sixth wedding day' of the German title counts the wedding itself as day one.
She had married on 25 May 1901, so the picture actually marks exactly five years: her fifth wedding anniversary.
Now let's look up at her face, framed by smooth reddish-brown hair.
She turns slightly and watches us with a searching, questioning look.
Around her closed lips hovers an expression that could be a smile, or could be hesitation.
Now down to the necklace.
The amber bead necklace hangs in large round beads down below her breasts.
Its warm orange glow answers the pink of her skin and brings warmth to the whole picture.
Her two hands cradle a rounded belly.
Although she appears to be pregnant, she was not when she painted it.
That rounded form sits at the very centre of the picture and holds our gaze.
The white cloth wrapped below her waist is painted in broad, quick, confident strokes.
Its cool, bluish white contrasts with her warm skin and seems to hold the figure up firmly from below.
Leaf-like marks are scattered across the pale green background.
In the lower right corner you can make out a few small lines of writing.
Nothing else distracts from the body and the face.
Painted in oil tempera on cardboard, the picture leaves out small details and reduces the body to simple, weighty shapes.
She learned a great deal from Post-Impressionist painters such as Cézanne and Gauguin.
She is counted among the earliest women painters to paint nude self-portraits.
As far as is known these pictures were not shown to outsiders in her lifetime, and she sold very few paintings at all.
The following November, shortly after giving birth to a daughter, she died at thirty-one.
In 1927 her museum opened in Bremen as the first museum devoted to a single woman artist.
Now step back and meet her eyes once more.
In a picture she may never have shown anyone, what is this thirty-year-old painter asking of herself, and what is she asking of us?
